newsitem.title: USA: NAFTA benefits exceed expectations - Fed economist.
newsitem.headline: NAFTA benefits exceed expectations - Fed economist.

text.p: The economic benefits of the North American Free Trade Agreement are likely to be far greater than previous studies of the pact suggested, a Federal Reserve Bank economist said Wednesday.

Chicago Fed economist Michael Kouparitsas said a new analysis of the trade pact shows it generating almost twice as much long-term economic output and trade flows for the United States, Canada and Mexico than estimated in previous studies.

The study shows the biggest benefit going to Mexico and its smaller economy, but the United States and Canada enjoy some gains in manufacturing, construction and services sectors, Kouparitsas said in an interview.

"NAFTA is making the (economic) pie much bigger and allows the pie to continue to grow," Kouparitsas said. He said the new study shows more economic activity under the trade pact than previous studies did because it uses a new "dynamic" model that looks at increases in capital that previous so-called "static" models failed to consider.

"Static models ignore the fact that capital accumulation is more efficient under free trade and therefore, understate the potential welfare and output gains that accrue from trade liberalization," the study said.
Kouparitsas said his study shows a slight increase in the overall U.S. trade deficit, but added it was more important to focus on overall productivity and economic growth.

"Even though we have a slight worsening of the overall trade deficit, we have additions to U.S. Gross Domestic Product which allows the United States to consume more and the welfare measurements show that people are better off," he said.

The study provides ammunition NAFTA supporters may need when Congress considers whether to give the Clinton administration so-called "fast track" authority to negotiate an expansion of NAFTA to include Chile. Many lawmakers are worried about persistent U.S. trade deficits with Mexico and the rest of the world, and those concerns are likely to factor into any debate.

Administration officials have said the fast track legislation will be a priority in the new Congress. It needs fast track authority so it can assure trading partners that Congress will not make major changes in any negotiated deal before voting on whether to accept or reject it.

Efforts to get fast track legislation failed in late 1995 in a dispute between the Republican-led Congress and the Democrat administration over authority to negotiate labor and environment issues in trade deals.
Outgoing Secretary of Commerce Mickey Kantor told reporters this week that he thought the two sides could reconcile their differences and agree to a bill.

"I would hope the Congress will respond to the president's entreaties in this area and provide fast track authority," Kantor said. He said he saw room for compromise on the labor and environment issues.
